setting: Marseilles, 24 February 1815
keepInMind: France is ruled again by a Bourbon king, Louis XVIII. Napoleon abdicated in 1814 and lives in exile on the island of Elba, and many people still miss him. The story opens as a merchant ship comes into harbour.

setting: Marseilles, the same day
keepInMind: Morrel has all but promised young Dantès command of the Pharaon, which the supercargo Danglars watched with open resentment. Dantès stopped at Elba on his dead captain's orders, and Danglars saw him handed a letter as well as a packet.

setting: The Catalan village outside Marseilles, the same afternoon
keepInMind: Dantès has hurried off to see Mercédès. Caderousse has told Danglars that a strapping Catalan 'cousin' always walks with her, and the two men have settled into the tavern arbour at La Réserve to wait for news.

setting: The arbour at La Réserve, moments later
keepInMind: Fernand has been refused by Mercédès and has just watched her walk off with Dantès. Danglars has heard that Dantès must go to Paris to deliver 'the letter which the grand marshal gave him', and says it gives him an idea.

setting: La Réserve, the next day
keepInMind: Danglars wrote a denunciation of Dantès with his left hand and tossed it, crumpled, into a corner, but Fernand picked it up and hurried off toward the city. Caderousse was too drunk to remember clearly.

setting: Marseilles, the same day, at a royalist betrothal feast in an aristocratic mansion
keepInMind: Dantès has been arrested at his wedding feast as a Bonapartist agent. Morrel has gone to plead with the deputy prosecutor, M. de Villefort, a known royalist.

setting: Marseilles, that afternoon
keepInMind: Villefort is about to marry into a fiercely royalist family, but his own father, the former Girondin and imperial senator Noirtier, is a Bonapartist whose name he has dropped. Renée begged him to be merciful, and the denunciation claims that Dantès carries a letter for Paris.

setting: Marseilles, that evening
keepInMind: Villefort burned the Elba letter, which was addressed to his own father, and made Dantès swear never to mention it, promising he would be held only until evening. Alone, Villefort told himself that the letter could make his fortune.

setting: The Saint-Méran house, the same evening
keepInMind: We go back a few hours to the moment Villefort left Dantès and hurried to his betrothed's house with a plan of his own.

setting: Paris: the king's private study in the Tuileries palace
keepInMind: Villefort is racing to Paris with Salvieux's letter of introduction, hoping to be the first to warn the king of a plot from Elba and so make his fortune. The Elba letter he burned was addressed to his own father.

setting: The Tuileries, a moment later
keepInMind: Villefort has just told Louis XVIII that Napoleon is arming ships on Elba, and the king brushed off the danger. Dandré, the minister of police, who had called the rumours nonsense, has appeared at the door looking pale. The police are also investigating a Bonapartist club in the Rue Saint-Jacques.

setting: Villefort's Paris hotel, the same day
keepInMind: The police are hunting a dark man of about fifty, in a blue frock-coat with black whiskers, over General Quesnel's death. They lost him near the Rue Coq-Héron, the street on the Elba letter. That man has just walked into Villefort's room: it is his father, Noirtier.

setting: Marseilles, spring 1815 and the months that follow
keepInMind: Noirtier predicted that Napoleon would reach Paris without a shot fired, and told his son to go home and keep quiet. Villefort alone knows why Dantès really vanished.

setting: The Château d'If, a year after the king's second restoration
keepInMind: Dantès threatened his jailer and was thrown into a lower dungeon 'with the madmen'. The jailer had warned him about an abbé who went mad offering the governor millions for his freedom.

setting: The Château d'If, the years that follow
keepInMind: The inspector's visit came to nothing: a note added to Dantès's file branded him a dangerous Bonapartist. Under a new governor he is known only as Number 34. The 'mad' Abbé Faria, who offers millions for his release, is Number 27.

setting: Dantès's cell
keepInMind: After four or five years without hearing any voice but his jailer's, Dantès has just seen his fellow tunneller climb up into his cell.

setting: The tunnel to the abbé's cell
keepInMind: Faria has told Dantès that he made his own pens, ink and paper and wrote a whole treatise in prison, and he is now taking him through the tunnel to see.

setting: The Château d'If, the next morning
keepInMind: Faria survived a terrible seizure but is now partly paralysed. He said he had something of the greatest importance to tell Dantès. Remember that the prison thinks him mad because he talks of a hidden treasure.

setting: The Château d'If
keepInMind: Faria has shared Cardinal Spada's secret, a treasure buried on the island of Monte Cristo, and named Dantès his heir. He has also warned that a third attack would kill him or leave him helpless.

setting: Faria's cell, that day
keepInMind: Faria is dead. His body has been sewn into a sack, and the governor has ordered it taken out at about ten or eleven tonight. No one knows of the tunnel.

setting: The sea off the Château d'If, that night
keepInMind: Dantès took Faria's place in the sack. Instead of burying him, the grave-diggers hurled him into the sea with a cannonball tied to his feet. He still has Faria's knife.

setting: Aboard the Genoese tartan La Jeune Amélie, bound for Leghorn, late February 1829
keepInMind: Dantès has passed himself off as a shipwrecked Maltese sailor on a vessel that is plainly a smuggler. It is fourteen years to the day since his arrest. He has renewed his vow of vengeance on Danglars, Fernand and Villefort.

setting: Leghorn, then at sea
keepInMind: The smugglers have picked the deserted island of Monte Cristo for their next rendezvous. Remember Spada's directions: count twenty rocks from the small creek to the east; there are two openings, and the treasure lies in the farthest angle of the second.
